title: R Madhavan Pushes Back on Propaganda Tag: 'Being Indian Cannot Be a Crime'
excerpt: The actor defends Dhurandhar and Rocketry against accusations of nationalistic propaganda, saying honest storytelling about Indian identity should not be controversial.
body:
• R Madhavan has pushed back against accusations that Dhurandhar and Rocketry: The Nambi Effect are propaganda films, calling the criticism baseless.
  • The actor said he has never been approached by any political party to promote them and that portraying Indian identity in cinema should not be treated as a crime.
  • Madhavan drew parallels between the Dhurandhar backlash and early criticism of Rang De Basanti and 3 Idiots, both of which faced skepticism before becoming modern classics.
  • His latest film GDN, a biopic of inventor GD Naidu, released theatrically on August 7 and marks his third consecutive portrayal of a real-life Indian figure.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=BKOVzHcjEIo

R Madhavan has responded to persistent criticism labeling his recent films as propaganda, saying he does not understand why expressing pride in Indian identity or showcasing the country's achievements on screen should invite accusations of political agenda. The actor addressed the debate in a conversation with Galatta Plus, drawing on his experience across two commercially successful but polarizing projects — the Dhurandhar franchise and Rocketry: The Nambi Effect.

Challenging the Propaganda Label

Madhavan played Ajay Sanyal, a spymaster character, in Aditya Dhar's Dhurandhar duology starring Ranveer Singh. Despite the franchise's blockbuster commercial run — Dhurandhar: The Revenge alone collected over ₹1,100 crore domestically — both films drew accusations from sections of the audience and critics of being nationalistic propaganda dressed up as entertainment.

The actor rejected the characterization outright. "I don't understand how being an Indian can be seen as a wrong thing," Madhavan said. "What does it mean by 'being overly Indian'? I don't know. Is it not okay to show myself as being 'too Indian'? That's not my conditioning; I showed that. This is not even a political statement."

"Dhurandhar was based in Pakistan. Good and bad things happen there as well, just as much as they do in India. So, I don't understand what the 'propaganda' in it is."

— R Madhavan, Actor

He pointed to the franchise's reception in Pakistan itself — where pirated versions of Dhurandhar circulated widely despite the film being banned — as evidence that the anti-Pakistan criticism does not hold up. "The videos of Pakistanis going berserk over Dhurandhar are all over," he said in a separate interview with Bollywood Hungama. "I want to ask all those who have accused the film of being anti-Pakistan, what do they have to say about the film's popularity in Pakistan?"

Rocketry and Staying True to Real People

Madhavan faced similar accusations after directing and starring in Rocketry: The Nambi Effect, his 2022 biopic on aerospace scientist Nambi Narayanan. Some critics argued the film presented an uncritically favorable view of its subject and of Indian nationalism more broadly.

Madhavan said he was simply being faithful to Narayanan's life as it actually was. "In Nambi sir's case, I only showed what happened in his life. How can I be honest with the story if I am afraid to show who he really is?" he said. "He is a person who goes to the temple. GD Naidu, on the other hand, is a nastik (atheist). So, we can't show such things in the movie. I have to be true to that character."

The distinction, Madhavan argued, is between honest biographical filmmaking and ideological agenda. "Because of that, one can't say that I don't believe in god or vice versa. I am an actor, and my job is to portray things as they are. My personal opinion is that I want to enhance all the good things about India. That cannot be a crime."

No Political Affiliations

Madhavan was direct about his political independence, saying no party — at the state or national level — has ever approached him for endorsement or membership. He said his public comments, including praise for Tamil Nadu's former Chief Minister MK Stalin, are driven by personal conviction, not political alignment.

"Everybody is a product of their conditioning. From a young age, I was taught that our country is the most important to us," he said. "If someone does something good, like Stalin sir for instance, I praise them immediately. I have decided that I will do only good, and if I have doubts about something, I won't talk about it."

On social media trolls who label Dhurandhar fans as "sanghis," Madhavan offered a practical response: check the accounts. "Look at their comment first, and then find out when they created their account, and how many followers they have. Through these steps, one can easily figure out if it's a bot or a paid account."

A Pattern of Early Backlash

Madhavan drew parallels between the Dhurandhar controversy and the reception of two earlier films he was part of — Rang De Basanti and 3 Idiots. Both faced early skepticism and negative reviews before being embraced as defining films of their era.

"From the beginning, I knew this was going to impact society. People will give it bad ratings at first," he told Filmfare. "The people who gave two ratings have become irrelevant. We are still in the industry. You're just missing the point, it's time to evolve."

What's Next

Madhavan's latest release, GDN, is a biographical drama based on the life of GD Naidu, the Coimbatore-based inventor and engineer often called the "Edison of India." The film, directed by Krishnakumar Ramakumar and co-written by Madhavan, released theatrically on August 7 with an ensemble cast including Sathyaraj, Jayaram, and Priyamani. It marks Madhavan's third consecutive portrayal of a real-life Indian figure, following Narayanan in Rocketry and his Dhurandhar spymaster character loosely modeled on National Security Advisor Ajit Doval.

For Indian diaspora audiences, Madhavan's broader argument — that depicting Indian identity and achievements in cinema is a legitimate creative choice, not propaganda — resonates with ongoing conversations about representation in global media. His films have consistently featured Indian characters operating on international stages, from espionage in Pakistan to space science rivalries, narratives that speak directly to the diaspora's interest in seeing India portrayed with complexity on screen.
